name: Deep Reddish Orange
lede: Deep reddish orange is the sixth and last of the oranges in Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's color nomenclature, a burnt, earthy orange defined by its goldfish, apple and topaz.

sections.title: A name built from its neighbors
sections.body:
Deep reddish orange is no. 81 among the oranges of Patrick Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*, the sixth and last step in a run of oranges that begins with Dutch orange (no. 76) [1]. Between them come [[buff-orange]], [[orpiment-orange]], brownish orange and [[reddish-orange]], so the series slides gradually from yellow toward red [1]. The name is plain description, a modifier stacked on a modifier, and there is no object, place or person behind it.

Other-language names are not part of the story here. The color belongs to the English-language mineralogical tradition that Werner started and Syme popularised [1].

sections.title: A recipe in words
sections.body:
Werner's scheme gave every color three real examples, one each from the animal, vegetable and mineral kingdoms. For no. 81 these are the lustre on a goldfish's scales, the Scarlet Leadington apple and a dark Brazilian topaz [2]. The goldfish and the apple were illustrated for Baty's reprint with a 1802 children's picture book and an 1829 pomological work; the mineral is shown with a lead-sulphide specimen drawn by James Sowerby in 1811 [2].

Syme also described each color as a mix of its neighbors. Deep reddish orange, he wrote, is Dutch orange mixed with much scarlet red, while the step before it, reddish orange, is buff orange with a considerable portion of tile red [2].

sections.title: The swatch and the system
sections.body:
Our swatch, #BB603C, comes from a scan of Werner's no. 81, so it carries the age of the printed plate and is approximate [3]. It is the only source for this name in our library; no later system adopted the term [3]. A modern ISCC-NBS description would call it a moderate reddish orange, 5.7 units away, and its nearest common name is [[sienna]], 7.4 units away [3]. In Munsell terms it sits near 1.0 YR 5.0/9.0, a medium-dark orange with moderate chroma [3].

So the modern eye sees a baked, earthy orange, like a fired tile or a rust-colored leaf.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 306 works, 1.3 per cent [4]. Indian painting leads again: 102 of 721 works carry it, 11 times the archive rate, and the Kalighat, Pahari and Rajput schools reach 23 of 96, 24 of 118 and 17 of 97 [4]. It is also common in the 1300s, with 11 of 251 paintings [4].

The largest single match is a ragamala leaf, *Sindhu Ragaputra*, of about 1680, where it covers 59 per cent of the picture [4]. In the West it turns up in [[painting:nga-41636|Saint Judas Thaddeus]] by Simone Martini, about 1315 [4], and in a [[painting:commons-Q52154241|self-portrait]] by Frederic Leighton of 1880 [4]. Pierre Bonnard and Albrecht Dürer are the painters who use it most often, four works each [4]. Its nearest company is [[vermilion]], [[burnt-orange]] and [[rust]] [4]. All of this is photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [4].
